Multi-wing Attractors and their Localization by Nambu Mechanics, and Chaos in Perturbed Harmonic Wells and Mixed Curvature Billiards

Abstract:

Phase space trajectories are fundamentally important for understanding and analyzing chaotic attractors. Though the topological properties of wings in chaotic attractors can be understood using tools like topological templates, linking numbers etc., but their emergence in the phase space can also be directly inferred from the geometry and relative orientations of Nambu surfaces (that are drawn using Nambu Hamiltonians) rather than from direct numerical solutions. These energy-like Hamiltonians can be extracted from the vector flow of the governing equations. Therefore, one can attribute the origin of wings in the phase space to the energy-like Nambu surfaces, giving a geometrical interpretation. In this thesis, we have implemented the Nambu mechanics (also known as generalized Hamiltonian mechanics) to explain the fundamental reason for the appearance of wing-like geometry of chaotic attractors in the phase space.&nbsp

This thesis also presents a focused investigation of a conservative chaotic system, specifically within the context of a Gaussian perturbed two-dimensional harmonic potential well. The Gaussian-perturbed system serves as a foundation for further inquiries rooted in the cymatics mechanism. In this study, we examine the effects of deformations induced by Gaussian perturbations on the development of chaotic dynamics. These deformations are produced through various configurations of Gaussian bumps in different geometric shapes, along with the modulation of the amplitude of the perturbed term shifting from positive to negative values.

The latter part of the thesis focuses on the important role of curvatures in billiard dynamics. When a boundary has varying curvature, it offers a unique setting to study the classical chaos. In this study, we introduce two geometrically distinct mixed curvature (both concave and convex curvature) billiards: Bean curve billiard and &nbspCassini curve billiard.&nbsp Our analysis of billiard flow diagrams confirms sensitivity to initial conditions - a defining feature of chaos. Poincar&eacute maps further show that the phase space intricately woven with regions of chaotic motion and stability islands. Additionally, we analyze the aforementioned billiard dynamics with presence of different shapes of obstacles/scatterers.
